items.summary: The Third Circuit's nonprecedential per curiam opinion filed November 5, 2026 in Kong Meng Xiong v. Attorney General (No. 25-3366) grants Xiong's petition for review of a Board of Immigration Appeals order that summarily dismissed his appeal as untimely. The court concluded that the EOIR letter mailed September 10, 2025 described the decision as the written decision and stated a 30-day appeal deadline from mailing, and that the Board received Xiong's notice of appeal on October 9, 2025, so the appeal should have been deemed timely filed. The court remanded the case for the Board to consider the substance of the appeal.

items.summary: On November 5, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit issued a non-precedential per curiam opinion affirming the Middle District of Pennsylvania's dismissal of pro se appellant Joseph Pilchesky's amended complaint against the Pennsylvania Office of the Attorney General and several of its officials. The court held that the Office and the officials in their official capacities were immune under the Eleventh Amendment, that Deputy Attorneys General McCarthy and Mahler were entitled to prosecutorial immunity on the individual-capacity claims, and that the remaining issues were forfeited or unsupported by the record. The court also found that the District Court had independently reviewed the Magistrate Judge's report before adopting it.

The court held that Fata did not plead the elements of a RICO claim or a TVPA forced-labor claim, did not state an equal protection class-of-one claim, and did not identify a protected liberty interest supporting a procedural due process claim. items.summary: The Tenth Circuit's November 5, 2026 order in In re: Tiger (No. 26-3220) denies Pidy T. Tiger's motion for authorization to file a second or successive 28 U.S.C. § 2254 habeas petition. The court found that the third claim did not meet the due diligence requirement of 28 U.S.C. § 2244(b)(2)(B)(i), because Tiger raised the underlying issue on direct appeal before filing his first petition, and that his first and second claims, even if proven, would not meet the standard of § 2244(b)(2)(B)(ii). Under § 2244(b)(3)(E), the denial is not appealable and is not subject to rehearing or certiorari.

items.summary: In this nonprecedential order, the Seventh Circuit affirmed a 120-month sentence imposed on Joseph Perkins after a jury convicted him of attempted enticement of a minor under 18 U.S.C. § 2422(b). Perkins had contended that the district judge should have given the jury an entrapment instruction, and the panel agreed with the district judge that the evidence did not support either governmental inducement or lack of predisposition. The order states that the sexual messages were initiated and repeated by Perkins, and that the FBI agent's posing account's communications were innocent in nature.
items.title: USA v. Joseph Perkins

items.summary: In this per curiam opinion, not recommended for publication, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit affirmed the drug convictions of Jamill McDonald, who had argued that his trial violated the Speedy Trial Act and that evidence from a search of his apartment should have been suppressed. The opinion recounts that officers responding to a reported burglary found a brick of cocaine in plain view during a safety sweep, after which they obtained a warrant and recovered additional narcotics, cash, scales, and phones. The court rejected both challenges and affirmed the judgment, and Judge Hermandorfer filed a separate opinion concurring in part and concurring in the judgment.
items.title: USA v. Jamill McDonald

items.summary: In this opinion, not recommended for publication, the Sixth Circuit affirmed a 24-month prison term imposed on Marcell Tillman after a second revocation of his supervised release, an upward variance above the Guidelines range of 4 to 10 months. Tillman had admitted to a state assault and battery violation arising from an incident that preceded a fatal shooting, and he challenged the sentence as procedurally and substantively unreasonable. The panel held that the district court adequately explained its reasons, did not rely on clearly erroneous facts, and imposed a substantively reasonable sentence.
items.title: USA v. Marcell Tillman

The opinion addresses claim construction disputes, the Board's weighing of copying and industry praise as objective indicia of nonobviousness, and the Board's finding that Google did not establish obviousness of claim 20 of the '075 patent and claim 27 of the '001 patent.
items.title: Google LLC v. DDC Technology, LLC

items.summary: In a nonprecedential per curiam opinion filed November 5, 2026, the Eleventh Circuit affirmed the Southern District of Florida's denial of pro se appellant Junior Jean Baptiste's motion to reduce his sentence under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(2) based on Amendment 821. The court held that U.S.S.G. § 4C1.1 does not apply to defendants who received an adjustment under § 3A1.1, and that Baptiste received two such adjustments. The court also found that any error from ruling before receipt of his reply brief was harmless.

items.summary: The Eleventh Circuit published an opinion in United States v. Andre Adams, Jr., appeal No. 24-14034, from the Middle District of Florida. The court affirmed Adams's convictions for possession with intent to distribute drugs, possession of a firearm in furtherance of a drug trafficking crime, and possession of a firearm as a convicted felon, and it affirmed his 228-month sentence, finding that the denial of a Franks hearing, the evidentiary rulings, the refusal of a requested jury instruction, and the denial of a judgment of acquittal were not erroneous.

items.summary: Senate amendment SA 1124, submitted by Mr. Lee on March 5, 2021, proposes to strike section 9901 of H.R. 1319 and insert a new provision adding section 602 to Title VI of the Social Security Act, which establishes a Coronavirus State Fiscal Recovery Fund. The text appropriates $219.8 billion for fiscal year 2021 for payments to states, territories, and Tribal governments, reserving $4.5 billion for territories, $20 billion for Tribal governments, and $195.3 billion for the 50 states and the District of Columbia, along with allocation formulas and a $50 million administrative appropriation. The amendment limits permitted uses of funds, bars use of funds to offset tax reductions or for pension fund deposits, and sets certification, reporting, and recoupment requirements; the source text is truncated before its regulations provision.
items.title: Text of Senate Amendment 1124

items.opening_verbatim:
OUR SINGULAR AMERICAN REVOLUTION

  The SPEAKER pro tempore. Under the Speaker's announced policy of
January 3, 2019, the gentleman from Texas (Mr. Gohmert) is recognized
for 60 minutes as the designee of the minority le
items.summary: Representative Gohmert, designated by the minority leader for a 60-minute special order, delivered remarks on the American and French revolutions, the distinction between a democracy and a republic, and infrastructure. He also criticized the conduct of former FBI Director Robert Mueller and the Special Counsel's investigation, citing the cases of Ted Stevens, Steven Hatfill, and Curt Weldon. He stated his view that no crime was committed in connection with the investigation's findings regarding Russian contacts with the Trump campaign.
items.title: OUR SINGULAR AMERICAN REVOLUTION

items.opening_verbatim:
STATEHOOD FOR THE DISTRICT OF COLUMBIA

  The SPEAKER pro tempore. Under the Speaker's announced policy of
January 3, 2019, the Chair recognizes the gentlewoman from the District
of Columbia (Ms. Norton) for 30 minutes.
  M
items.summary: Ms. Norton, the gentlewoman from the District of Columbia, spoke for 30 minutes on statehood for the District of Columbia in advance of Memorial Day. She stated that District residents have served in every war and do not have full voting representation, and she noted that the House passed H.R. 1 in March, which includes findings and provisions on D.C. statehood. She also stated that the statehood bill had 204 cosponsors and cited endorsements from national organizations.
items.title: STATEHOOD FOR THE DISTRICT OF COLUMBIA

items.summary: Senators Wicker, Markey, and Thune spoke on the Senate floor about S. 151, the Telephone Robocall Abuse Criminal Enforcement and Deterrence Act (TRACED Act), before its final passage vote. Wicker stated that the bill would give the FCC tools to address robocall violators, require phone companies to authenticate calls, and involve the Attorney General in prosecuting robocall violations. Markey cited an estimated 48 billion robocalls received by consumers in 2018 and described the bill's three elements as call authentication, call blocking, and extending the FCC's penalty window from 1 year to 3 years.

items.summary: The Senate considered S. 151 with a committee amendment that would amend Section 227 of the Communications Act of 1934 to add civil forfeiture penalties for robocall violations, including an additional penalty of up to $10,000 for violations committed with intent. The text sets limitation periods of 1 year for general violations and 3 years for intentional violations, requires an annual FCC report to Congress on robocall and spoofed-call enforcement, and requires providers to implement the STIR/SHAKEN call authentication framework within 18 months of enactment unless the FCC makes specified determinations. items.summary: Senate amendment SA 250, proposed by Senator McConnell for Senator Shelby and Senator Leahy, would strike all text after the enacting clause of H.R. 2157, a supplemental appropriations bill for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2019, and insert new provisions. The amendment provides appropriations for agricultural and disaster-related programs, including $3,005,442,000 for the Office of the Secretary for crop and tree losses, $480,000,000 for the Emergency Forest Restoration Program, $558,000,000 for the Emergency Conservation Program, $435,000,000 for watershed and flood prevention operations, and $150,000,000 for rural community facilities grants. Section 103 makes persons or legal entities with average adjusted gross income above $900,000 ineligible for Market Facilitation Program payments, unless at least 75 percent of their adjusted gross income is derived from farming, ranching, or forestry related activities.

items.summary: The Senate Record of March 5, 2021 prints SA 1117, submitted by Senator Daines and Senator Lankford, which would strike section 9901 through title X of H.R. 1319 and insert provisions establishing Coronavirus State and Local Fiscal Recovery Funds under title VI of the Social Security Act. The proposed text appropriates $219,800,000,000 for payments to states, territories, and Tribal governments, reserving $4,500,000,000 for territories, $20,000,000,000 for Tribal governments, and $195,300,000,000 for the 50 states and the District of Columbia, with allocation and minimum-payment rules. It also restricts the use of the funds, including offsetting net tax revenue reductions and deposits into pension funds, and sets certification, reporting, and recoupment requirements, with the source text truncated.

The text appropriates $219.8 billion for fiscal year 2021, available through December 31, 2024, with reserved amounts of $4.5 billion for territories, $20 billion for Tribal governments, and $195.3 billion for the 50 states and the District of Columbia, and limits fund uses to COVID-19 response, related economic impacts, and government services affected by revenue reductions. items.summary: Ms. Collins and cosponsors submitted amendment SA 1151, intended to be proposed to amendment SA 891 to H.R. 1319 and ordered to lie on the table, which proposes a substitute in lieu of the matter to be inserted. Its table of contents lists provisions across Titles I through VI for the Committees on Agriculture, Banking, Finance, Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, and Small Business and Entrepreneurship. The text includes extending SNAP benefit values from June 30, 2021 to September 30, 2021 with $1.15 billion in administrative funding, $25 million for SNAP online purchasing, $1 billion for nutrition grants to the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, Puerto Rico, and American Samoa, and a WIC cash-value voucher increase up to $35 with $490 million, along with vaccine, testing, stockpile, mental health, school, child care, and paycheck protection program provisions, and the excerpt ends partway through the text.

items.summary: Ms. Collins and cosponsors proposed amendment SA 1242 to amendment SA 891 to H.R. 1319 as a substitute in lieu of the matter to be inserted. Its table of contents reduces Title IV to three sections, covering public health programs (Sec. 4001), schools (Sec. 4101), and child care (Sec. 4201), while retaining the agriculture, finance, small business, and homeland security titles. The Title I text matches the SNAP, WIC, and nutrition provisions described in SA 1151, including the SNAP benefit extension to September 30, 2021, $1.15 billion for SNAP administrative expenses, and a WIC cash-value voucher increase up to $35 with $490 million, and the excerpt is truncated in the source.

items.summary: Mr. Rubio submitted amendment SA 1296, intended to be proposed to amendment SA 891 to H.R. 1319 and ordered to lie on the table, which would add a section titled Medical Manufacturing Economic Development and Sustainability at the end of subtitle G of title IX. The proposed Internal Revenue Code Subchapter AA would allow a credit of 40 percent (60 percent for qualified repatriated pharmaceutical manufacturing facilities) of certain wages, employee fringe benefit expenses, and depreciation for medical product manufacturing facilities in economically distressed zones, and a credit of 30 percent (5 percent for related persons) for qualified products and services acquired from those zones. The provision also allows an election to expense certain facility property and defines economically distressed zones as census tracts with a poverty rate of at least 35 percent for each of the five most recent calendar years or meeting alternative criteria, and the excerpt is truncated in the source.

items.summary: Senate amendment SA 1336, submitted by Mr. Moran to amendment SA 891 to H.R. 1319, proposes replacing section 2 with a table of contents and inserting provisions under Title I (Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions), Title II (Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs), and Title III (Committee on Finance). The Title I provisions appropriate $7,500,000,000 to the CDC for COVID-19 vaccine activities, $1,000,000,000 for vaccine confidence activities, $6,050,000,000 for vaccine supply chain activities, $500,000,000 for FDA activities, and $47,800,000,000 for COVID-19 testing, contact tracing, and mitigation. The amendment also amends the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act to treat individuals receiving unemployment compensation during 2021 as meeting certain requirements and to disregard household income above 133 percent of the poverty line for that purpose.

items.summary: Senate amendment SA 1339, submitted by Mr. Rubio and Mr. Lee to amendment SA 891 to H.R. 1319, would strike part 2 of subtitle G of title IX and insert Child Tax Credit provisions for 2021. items.summary: Senate amendment SA 1380, submitted by Mr. Lee and Mr. Rubio to amendment SA 891 to H.R. 1319, would strike part 2 of subtitle G of title IX through the end of part 4 and insert Child Tax Credit provisions for 2021. This version sets the credit at $3,300 per qualifying child ($4,100 for children under age 6), with the same age, income phaseout, and $50-per-$1,000 reduction provisions as amendment SA 1339. It also establishes the advance payment program under Internal Revenue Code section 7527A, including periodic payments, an online portal, and written notice of payments to taxpayers by January 31 of the following year.

items.summary: Amendment SA 1381, proposed by Lee and Rubio to amendment SA 891 to H.R. 1319, would strike parts 2 through 4 of subtitle G of title IX and insert a new Part 2 on the child tax credit. The inserted text adds special rules for 2021 taxable years to Section 24 of the Internal Revenue Code, including a $3,300 credit amount ($4,200 for children under age 6), a reduction based on modified adjusted gross income with threshold amounts of $150,000, $112,500, and $75,000, and treatment of 17-year-olds as qualifying children. It also adds Section 7527A, which directs the Secretary to establish periodic advance payments of the credit and an online portal for electing out of payments and submitting updated information.

items.summary: Amendment SA 1398, proposed by Schumer to amendment SA 891 to H.R. 1319, revises that amendment by setting minimum funding percentages for listed purposes, reducing a dollar figure on page 33 from $125,804,800,000 to $122,774,800,000, and adding Section 2014 to appropriate $2,580,000,000 for part B grants, $200,000,000 for preschool grants, and $250,000,000 for infants and toddlers under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act. It also amends the Railroad Unemployment Insurance Act and Section 2112 of the CARES Act to replace the March 14, 2021 dates with September 6, 2021, and extends certain railroad unemployment benefit durations. The amendment further adds Section 4015, which deems covered Federal employees diagnosed with COVID-19 between January 27, 2020 and January 27, 2023 to have an injury caused by exposure to the novel coronavirus for workers' compensation claims under subchapter I of chapter 81 of title 5, United States Code, excluding employees who are exclusively teleworking during a covered exposure period.

items.summary: The FAA proposes to supersede Airworthiness Directive (AD) 2024-15-04, which applies to certain Dassault Aviation Model FALCON 7X airplanes. AD 2024-15-04 requires revising the existing maintenance or inspection program, as applicable, to incorporate new or more restrictive airworthiness limitations. Since the FAA issued AD 2024-15-04, the FAA has determined that new or more restrictive airworthiness limitations are necessary. This proposed AD would continue to require certain actions in AD 2024-15-04 and would require revising the existing maintenance or inspection program, as applicable, to incorporate new or more restrictive airworthiness limitations. The FAA is proposing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products.

items.opening_verbatim: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE Food and Nutrition Administration 7 CFR Part 246 [FNA-2026-0595] RIN 0584-AE85 Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC): Online Ordering and Transactions and Food Delivery Revis
items.summary: This final rule considers public comments submitted in response to the proposed rule to remove barriers to online ordering and internet-based transactions in the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) published on February 23, 2023. USDA FNA is issuing this regulatory action to support State innovation and develop and implement modernized systems, while underscoring program integrity. It allows for the use of new technologies to improve the WIC shopping experience while increasing access to healthy foods for WIC participants. This final rule also complements the Program's complete transition to electronic benefit transfer (EBT) by streamlining and modernizing certain WIC food delivery regulations to support current technology and future innovation, and introduces measures to support a modern, data-driven program that uses new technologies for food delivery.
items.title: Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC): Online Ordering and Transactions and Food Delivery Revisions To Meet the Needs of a Modern, Data-Driven Program

items.summary: The Department of Labor (DOL or the Department) is issuing this final rule to remove the onerous and legally questionable affirmative action requirements that were previously imposed by the Department on Registered Apprenticeship program sponsors. This final rule also streamlines and simplifies nondiscrimination obligations for all program sponsors, while clarifying that sponsors are accountable for compliance with Federal and State nondiscrimination protections. It also makes conforming, technical changes to the Department's regulation that addresses Labor Standards for the Registration of Apprenticeship Programs.
items.title: Prohibiting Illegal Discrimination in Registered Apprenticeship Programs

items.summary: We, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (Service), announce technical corrections for 43 wildlife and plant species under the Endangered Species Act of 1973, as amended (Act). For 7 wildlife species and 30 plant species that predominately occur in California and Nevada, we are revising the List of Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and the List of Endangered and Threatened Plants (“the Lists”) to reflect the current scientifically accepted taxonomy and nomenclature of these species. We are also making commensurate revisions to the applicable critical habitat sections. Further, for six wildlife species occurring within the United States and territories, we are correcting errors in the Lists made in previous publications. The taxonomic, nomenclatural, and orthographic revisions and the corrections of publication errors are editorial in nature and involve no substantive changes to the Lists or any applicable regulations.
items.title: Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Technical Corrections for 43 Wildlife and Plant Species on the Lists of Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants

items.summary: The North Pacific Fishery Management Council (Council) submitted amendment 128 to the Fishery Management Plan (FMP) for Groundfish of the Bering Sea and Aleutian Islands Management Area (BSAI FMP) and amendment 116 to the FMP for Groundfish fisheries of the Gulf of Alaska (GOA FMP) to the Secretary of Commerce for review. If approved, these amendments would increase operational flexibility to allow vessels fishing for sablefish with fixed gear under the Individual Fishing Quota (IFQ) Program or Western Alaska Community Development (CDQ) Program to release sablefish and would revise the annual allocation process to account for sablefish discards. This action is intended to promote the goals and objectives of the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act (Magnuson-Stevens Act), the BSAI and GOA FMPs, and other applicable laws.
items.title: Fisheries of the Exclusive Economic Zone Off Alaska; Amendment 128 to the FMP for Groundfish of the Bering Sea and Aleutian Islands Management Area and Amendment 116 to the FMP for the Groundfish Fisheries of the Gulf of Alaska; Small Sablefish Release

items.summary: The Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) is establishing a specific listing and DEA Controlled Substances Code Number (drug code) for 1-(3-chlorophenyl)-2-(methylamino)propan-1-one (3-chloromethcathinone; 3-CMC) in schedule I of the Controlled Substances Act (CSA). Although 3-chloromethcathinone is not specifically listed in schedule I of the CSA with its own unique drug code, it is a schedule I controlled substances in the United States because it is a positional isomer of 4-chloromethcathinone, which is a schedule I hallucinogen. Therefore, DEA is simply amending the schedule I hallucinogenic substances list in its regulations to separately include 3-chloromethcathinone.

items.opening_verbatim: DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH AND HUMAN SERVICES Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services 42 CFR Parts 413, 416, 419, 427, and 488 [CMS-1850-FC] RIN 0938-AV83 Medicare Program: Hospital Outpatient Prospective Payment and Ambulatory Surgical Center P
items.summary: This final rule with comment period revises the Medicare Hospital Outpatient Prospective Payment System (OPPS) and the Medicare Ambulatory Surgical Center (ASC) payment system for calendar year 2027 based on our continuing experience with these systems. We also describe the changes to the amounts and factors used to determine the payment rates for Medicare services paid under the OPPS and those paid under the ASC payment systems. In addition, this final rule with comment period updates and refines the requirements for the Hospital Outpatient Quality Reporting Program and the Ambulatory Surgical Center Quality Reporting Program. There are no changes to the Rural Emergency Hospital Quality Reporting Program. We finalized the expansion of the prior authorization requirement to include additional Botulinum Toxin Injection services. We also finalized implementation of certain provisions of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026, for off-campus outpatient departments of a provider. In addition, this final rule with comment period announces notices of closure of teaching hospitals and opportunities to apply for available slots. [official summary truncated; see source]

items.opening_verbatim: SECURITIES AND EXCHANGE COMMISSION 17 CFR Parts 270, 275, and 279 [Release Nos. IA-7035; IC-36380; File No. S7-2026-01] RIN 3235-AN39 Amendments to the “Small Business” and “Small Organization” Definitions for Investment Companies and Inves
items.summary: The Securities and Exchange Commission (the “Commission” or the “SEC”) is amending the definitions of “small business” and “small organization” (collectively, “small entities”) that are used in connection with Commission rulemaking under the Investment Company Act of 1940 (the “Investment Company Act”) and the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 (the “Advisers Act”). These definitions concern regulatory requirements applicable to registered investment companies and business development companies (collectively, “funds”) as well as investment advisers. The definitions are used specifically for purposes of the Regulatory Flexibility Act (the “RFA”), which requires the Commission to consider the impact of its regulations on small entities. The amendments are designed to modernize the definitions, by increasing certain asset-based thresholds, including a mechanism for periodic future inflation adjustments, and eliminating the threshold based on total assets for advisers. [official summary truncated; see source]
items.title: Amendments to the “Small Business” and “Small Organization” Definitions for Investment Companies and Investment Advisers for Purposes of the Regulatory Flexibility Act

items.opening_verbatim: Title 3— The President Proclamation 11078 of November 3, 2026 Anti-Communism Week, 2026 By the President of the United States of America A Proclamation For more than a century, human freedom has been threatened by communist and socialist id
items.summary: Proclamation 11078, dated November 3, 2026, designates the week of November 1 through November 7, 2026 as Anti-Communism Week. The proclamation describes communist and socialist ideologies as threats to individual liberty, and it references the effects of state control over thought, creativity, and political expression. It calls on Americans to defend the Constitution and the nation's founding principles against those ideologies during the observance.
items.title: Anti-Communism Week, 2026

items.opening_verbatim: Proclamation 11079 of November 3, 2026 The American Declaration of Freedom in Space By the President of the United States of America A Proclamation It is America's destiny to explore and expand our frontiers beyond Earth to the farthest dep
items.summary: Proclamation 11079, dated November 3, 2026, is titled "The American Declaration of Freedom in Space." It proclaims that the solar system and all of outer space beyond Earth are open to exploration, development, use, and the establishment of a permanent presence by American citizens, consistent with United States law and the country's international obligations. The document also references the Artemis II mission's April flight around the Moon, the planned Artemis III test campaign next summer, and a goal of returning to the Moon by 2028.
items.title: The American Declaration of Freedom in Space

items.summary: The reported bill, titled the Comprehensive Health and Integrity in Licensing and Documentation Act of 2026 (CHILD Act of 2026), amends Section 5(9)(B) of the National Child Protection Act of 1993 to expand the definition of covered individual. The amended definition would include persons employed by, contracting with, or volunteering with an entity under contract with a qualified entity, as well as persons who are or seek to be licensed or certified by a qualified entity. The bill was reported with an amendment and committed to the Committee of the Whole House on November 5, 2026.
items.title: 119 HR 3100 RH: Comprehensive Health and Integrity in Licensing and Documentation Act of 2026

items.opening_verbatim: IB Union Calendar No. 768 119th CONGRESS 2d Session H. R. 3978 [Report No. 119–871] IN THE HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES June 12, 2025 Mr. Latta (for himself and Mr. Peters ) introduced the following bill; which was referred to the Committee on
items.summary: The reported bill, the Nuclear REFUEL (Recycling Efficient Fuels Utilizing Expedited Licensing) Act, amends the definition of production facility in Section 11 v. of the Atomic Energy Act of 1954. The amendment adds reprocessing of spent nuclear fuel in a manner that does not isolate plutonium to the activities listed in that definition, and it inserts the word reprocessing into the existing text on uranium enrichment. The bill was reported with an amendment and committed to the Committee of the Whole House on November 5, 2026.
items.title: 119 HR 3978 RH: Nuclear REFUEL (Recycling Efficient Fuels Utilizing Expedited Licensing) Act

items.opening_verbatim: IB Union Calendar No. 769 119th CONGRESS 2d Session H. R. 5549 [Report No. 119–872] IN THE HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES September 23, 2025 Mr. Griffith (for himself, Ms. Schrier , and Mr. Veasey ) introduced the following bill; which was referr
items.summary: The bill, titled the Efficient Nuclear Licensing Hearings Act, amends the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 to change hearing procedures for nuclear facility licensing. It allows the Nuclear Regulatory Commission to issue construction permits, operating licenses, and related amendments without a hearing when no affected person requests one, after thirty days notice and Federal Register publication. The bill also requires informal adjudicatory procedures for any hearing held, conditions uranium enrichment facility hearings on a request from an affected person, and applies to pending applications on enactment.
items.title: 119 HR 5549 RH: Efficient Nuclear Licensing Hearings Act

items.opening_verbatim: IB Union Calendar No. 766 119th CONGRESS 2d Session H. R. 5723 [Report No. 119–869] IN THE HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES October 8, 2025 Mr. Takano introduced the following bill; which was referred to the Committee on Veterans' Affairs November
items.summary: The reported bill, the Fraud Reduction And Uncovering Deception in VA Disability Exams Act (FRAUD in VA Disability Exams Act), adds Section 5322 to chapter 53 of title 38, United States Code. That section directs the Secretary of Veterans Affairs to identify fraud in disability benefit questionnaire forms, establish a process for claims processors to report suspected fraud to the Office of Inspector General, direct routine audits, and inform claimants when information is insufficient to assign a rating, with an annual report to the Veterans' Affairs committees. The bill also amends Section 312 of title 38 to authorize the Inspector General to deposit funds from undercover investigations in designated accounts or financial institutions, requires quarterly audits and an annual report by November 30, and takes effect 90 days after enactment.
items.title: 119 HR 5723 RH: Fraud Reduction And Uncovering Deception in VA Disability Exams Act

items.opening_verbatim: IB Union Calendar No. 771 119th CONGRESS 2d Session H. R. 9084 [Report No. 119–874] IN THE HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES June 2, 2026 Ms. Castor of Florida introduced the following bill; which was referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce
items.summary: The reported bill, the Department of Energy Nuclear Transparency Act, requires the Secretary of Energy to post public announcements on a Department of Energy website within 72 hours of specified actions regarding covered DOE nuclear facilities of Hazard Category 1, 2, and 3. The required announcements cover alterations to directives and safety standards, issuance of preliminary documented safety analyses or documented safety analyses (which may be modified to remove commercially sensitive, classified, or controlled information), and agreements to authorize such facilities, including any applicable conditions. The bill also requires the Secretary to submit an annual report by January 31 to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce and the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources detailing authorization activities from the previous calendar year.
items.title: 119 HR 9084 RH: Department of Energy Nuclear Transparency Act

items.opening_verbatim: IB Union Calendar No. 767 119th CONGRESS 2d Session H. R. 9605 [Report No. 119–870] IN THE HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES July 9, 2026 Mr. Grothman introduced the following bill; which was referred to the Committee on Education and Workforce Nove
items.summary: The reported bill, the Less Bureaucracy, Better Foreign Medical Accreditation Act, transfers from the Secretary of Education to the Secretary of Health and Human Services all functions related to the National Committee on Foreign Medical Education and Accreditation. The bill also transfers related personnel, assets, contracts, records, and unexpended appropriations, directs the Director of the Office of Management and Budget to ensure no net increase in full-time equivalent employees, and sets out savings, continuation of suits, and reference-substitution provisions. The transfer takes effect six months after enactment, with early implementation permitted, and the bill was committed to the Committee of the Whole House on November 5, 2026.
items.title: 119 HR 9605 RH: Less Bureaucracy, Better Foreign Medical Accreditation Act

items.opening_verbatim: IB Union Calendar No. 772 119th CONGRESS 2d Session H. R. 9612 [Report No. 119–875] IN THE HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES July 9, 2026 Mr. Fry (for himself, Ms. Schrier , and Mrs. Houchin ) introduced the following bill; which was referred to the
items.summary: H.R. 9612, the American Enrichment Deployment Act, was introduced on July 9, 2026, referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, and reported with an amendment on November 5, 2026 (Report No. 119-875). The bill amends Section 193 of the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 to permit construction of a uranium enrichment facility before a license is issued under sections 53 and 63, under the same terms applicable to other licensed fuel cycle facilities, while stating that this does not limit the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's authority to deny a license application. It directs the Commission to issue or revise implementing regulations within 180 days of enactment and provides that the National Environmental Policy Act, hearing rights under section 189, and Commission inspection authority are not affected.
items.title: 119 HR 9612 RH: American Enrichment Deployment Act

items.opening_verbatim: IB Union Calendar No. 774 119th CONGRESS 2d Session H. R. 9613 [Report No. 119–877] IN THE HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES July 9, 2026 Mrs. Harshbarger (for herself and Mr. Goldman of Texas ) introduced the following bill; which was referred to t
items.summary: H.R. 9613, the Nuclear Advisory Committee Reform Act, was introduced on July 9, 2026 by Representative Harshbarger, referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, and reported with an amendment on November 5, 2026 (Report No. 119-877). The bill amends Section 29 of the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 to set the Advisory Committee on Reactor Safeguards at a maximum of 15 members appointed by the Commission, limit members to two four-year terms unless the Commission determines there is a compelling need for continued service, and specify the Committee's review duties and areas of focus. It also permits the Committee to decline review of certain license applications under section 182(b) and makes conforming amendments to sections 163 and 192 of the Act.
items.title: 119 HR 9613 RH: Nuclear Advisory Committee Reform Act

items.opening_verbatim: IB Union Calendar No. 773 119th CONGRESS 2d Session H. R. 9614 [Report No. 119–876] IN THE HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES July 9, 2026 Mr. Menendez introduced the following bill; which was referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce November
items.summary: H.R. 9614, the NRC Staff Pay Alignment Act, was introduced on July 9, 2026 by Representative Menendez, referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, and committed to the Committee of the Whole House on November 5, 2026 (Report No. 119-876). The bill amends Section 161B of the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 to authorize the Chairman to fix the compensation of career appointees at a rate not greater than 110 percent of the maximum basic pay for Senior Executive Service positions within the Commission. It also adds the number of career appointees with compensation fixed under this authority to the required reporting, and makes a conforming amendment to the Government Accountability Office report provision in section 502(b) of the ADVANCE Act of 2024.
items.title: 119 HR 9614 RH: NRC Staff Pay Alignment Act
